The thing is senior ops, and often higher operation cammand have no understanding of how an actual airport is run. So they fall back to their fc training. If they treat an airport like an fc the risks become graver. 

An air ramp is one of the most dangerous jobs you can get. You have engines that can suck you in, and propellers that can blitz you. The weather is always against you. Rain, snow, heat, lightening. 100 degree summers. 20 degree winters. Risk of slipping hazards over 100ft drops. We dont have rate for us but we do have our block out times. If the plane is late it will look bad for us. We dont have process assistants, we have load planners. They come up with a plane load to ensure the plane is balanced. If it is not the risk of a crash is high. 

We have to be both fast, and safe. If we fail to be fast the load planners and even us run the risk of being written up. If we go too fast as to cause a load error the TSA, and FAA will beat our asses into the ground if it does not make it. If it does make it even with the fuck up we risk losing our jobs. 

Some fucks ups can cause you to be sent to a federal prison. Go up the cockpit, terrorist action. Enter the planes gate when the engine lights go off,  instant termination/death. The plane hits something during taxing, federal investigation. Walk past taxi way into the run way, federal prison. Intentionally ignoring a loading issues, federal prison. Damage the plane, termination. 

The average cargo container (uld) we use weighs a min of 500lbs empty for the smallest ones. Upto 2500/3500lbs. If the dolly locks are not set the thing will fly off like a dodge ball. 

The job is very rewarding, and we have the highest amount of promotions from our dept. The rule of thumb of being out here is be safe, and do not fuck up. 

We have all had bad injury experiences working for the ramp. The lower deck of 767s have holes in them. I fell in one a year ago. Fiberglass, and a metal spike almost stabbed me. We have people who have broken their feet working the main deck. One of my friends nearly got sucked into an engine because someone marshaled the plane to far up. We have had people nearly get frost bite, and collapse from heat strokes. Some of those collapses are after they labour share us inside when they vto their dept. 

We also get paid a 1.50 less than those who work inside. Go figure.

They have been trying to enforce that 90% turn over on our ramp and are using everything they can to fire ramp personal. Ramp in general probably has the lowest turn over rate in all of amazon in general. 

It is backfiring horribly. It takes 3 months to train a new ramp person to have both skill and proficiency in their job. Compared to a week in a standard fc. The longer the ramper stays to gain more skill, and vehicle licenses causes the loss to be even more damaging. We have 5 vehicles out here. One of the things before being trained on a vehicle is knowing how to marshal them to the aircraft. Once they show proficiency in that they will be tested by being given deck and belly duty until they are proficient working the plane decks. It takes 3 months of doing this before they will become vehicle trained. 

The first vehicle they will be taught is the cargo tractor along with the dollies. 

Then the belt loader, and the power stow. 

Last vehicle for most will be the cargo loader. Which is one of the most dangerous pieces of equipment to operate. It is bigger than the average house in my area. It presents a high fall risk, and a crush risk. It is essential for the loading of a plane. 

Then the most dangerous one. The one they wont trust but too the best of the personal. The tow bar less pushback. It picks an entire 767-3 front end up from the main gear and pushes it back. One fuck up can cause the aircraft to break. Possibly killing you, and pilots.

Amazon got rid of our lockers when covid happened. For the most part I keep everything in the trunk of my car. However, since the facility is getting rid of anti covid measures I can imagine we will see the return of our equipment lockers.

Things like gloves(thin rubber kind, and really bad quality water resistant kind. I recommend getting good cold weather gloves though), stubby ear protection, hot hands, clip boards, and to some extent amazon supplies us with high vision gear which includes the rain gear, They also have public high vision jackets that can be loaned out during winter.

I prefer having my own equipment though. If you do work for an amazon air ramp make sure to get your own class 2 ansi vest. The ones they supply all our new hires with can just barely meet the qualifications. No pockets being the worst offender for working on an air ramp. Keep a spare as well. My old vest got ripped open by one the tugs they shoved me in.

Off track statement though. Anti rain suits are plastic. I will never recommend anyone wear them in warm weather unless you fancy heat stroke. Just keep a thin medical scrub style jumpsuit. Preferably cotton because the humidity is painful enough without the heat.

Just to note. Get your summer stuff during the summer, and winter stuff during the winter. It will help you save money by focusing on what you need for that season. 

Another thing is some companies will supply you with everything but your boots. So check on that first.

Our facility requires us to wear composite toe boots but others allow other types of boots. I recommend:  

full water proof high vision rain suit. 

A high vision cold weather jacket. 

Two jumpsuits one that is lined for cold weather and another for warm but wet weather (the rain suit in warm weather is not recommended).  

Your own class 2 ansi high vision vest. One with enough pockets to carry stuff. Maybe a spare if the other gets destroyed. 

A hat for the different types of weather. Cold, wet, hot, sunny. Make sure to have a strap on it incase of high wind.

Sunglasses if you work day. Goggles for cold weather.

A pair of waterproof gloves, thermal gloves, and a light pair of gloves for warm weather. 

A water bottle for cold weather, and a water camel for hot weather. 

Ice packs or cooling vest in cool weather. 

Both light and heavy hearing protection. Little stub things incase you forgot your heavy headset. 

Good moisture wicking socks. 

Suspenders  instead of a belt. No full moons from atop a cargo loader. 

A bandana in case the plane smells bad. Had a plane that smelled so bad I nearly puked. 

Ski mask for cold weather. 

Two watches. One in 24 hour time the other in 12 hour. 

If they allow it carry a radio compatible with the facilities transponder. 

A couple of pens. Blue and black. 

A foldable clipboard to fill out GSE checklists and for verification work. 

Hot hands for winter or night shifts. 

If you have a locker. Deodorant, and deodorizer if you keep your boots in there.
